256 REVIEWS OF BOOKS A STUDY OF HISTORY. By Arnold J. Toynbee. Abridgment of Vols. VII-X by D. C. Somer- vell. New York: Oxford University Press, 1957. Pp. 393. $5.00. TOYNBEE AND HISTORY: CRITICAL ESSAYS AND REVIEWS. Edited by M. F. Ashley Montagu. Boston: Porter Sargent, 1956. Pp. 385. $5.00. Mr. Somervell here completes the consider- able task of extracting the essential Toynbee theory from the vast mass of the last four vol- umes (reviewed by Garrett Mattingly, Journal, XXVIII [1956], 176-77). One must say imme- diately that it could not have been a constant delight. The final volumes are terrifying in their prolixity and obscure jargon. Here in the abridgment one is spared much of this some- times nightmare use of the English language. The Toynbeean conversion to the conviction of the primacy of religion is seen in a relatively clear light. Approving heartily, Toynbee praises his collaborator for his "wonderfully good eye" for this kind of thing and judges it "a boon to be abbreviated in a first-rate Abridgement" (p. v). Somervell, for his part, has accounted it no great trick: "I just moved steadily forward," he remarked recently, "saying to myself, This is rather dull, cut it out. Or, this is interesting, put it in, with abbreviation. Or, this is essential, put it in, word for word" (New York Times Book Review, February 10, 1957, p. 8). The various chapters deal with universal states, universal churches, heroic ages, contacts between civilizations in space, contacts between civilizations in time, law and freedom in history, and the prospects of Western civilization. The general thesis is sufficiently well known by now not to require one more unsatisfactory putting- down here. By and large, there does not seem to be any great hope for us, and, indeed, Toyn- bee is not much interested in us as such. He is concerned rather with the salvation of mankind through absorption in some syncretic religion and with "fulfilling the true end of Man by glorifying God and enjoying Him once again" (p. 349). And if all this is somewhat underplayed in the abridged version, the reader will not be unaware that this is the real conclusion and the real purpose of writing this book. As historian, Toynbee continues to go through the secular motions (how unfair this phrase is when one con- siders the fantastic mountain of learning he builds!), but plainly he has left us poor seekers after tiny parochial "truths" far down below and has himself soared off in time and space. The quaint detailed references to the economic plight of Wall Street shorthand typists in A.D. 1949 (p. 336) or the very severe subjective stric- tures passed on the policies of the state of Israel in A.D. 1948 (pp. 171-79) do not alter the fact that, however unwilling he may be to admit it, the author is pretty much convinced that the human tragedy approaches its historical end. In effect, he is saying farewell to the world as we know it. This is not to suggest that the book will fail to fascinate readers not in search of religious teleologies. It is replete with absorbing essays, even if (through simple ignorance) you may feel you can follow very few of them at all critically. And yet one must say frankly that if the thesis comes through at the cost of less agony here than in the original, much-perhaps most-of what appeals in Arnold Toynbee is lost. No abridgment will do as a substitute for the in- spired flights of the original. There is no sugges- tion here of that entrancing and slightly horri- fying section "Acknowledgements and Thanks" in Volume X. Somervell has done his best, but Toynbee just is not "completed" (as the dust jacket announces) without Mother, Uncle Paget, Dr. Sylvia Payne (who "helped me, in a time of great personal trouble, to find a way through the dark wood which I could not have found by myself" [X, 237]), and Fra Angelico. Still, here are the general propositions, the laws, the vast judgments. This writer has not the slightest notion of what over-all historical worth they may be. From time to time one finds one's self rejecting this or that as unfair or merely contrary to what one thinks one already knows. But it is a feeble protest. The work as a whole escapes one. It certainly is not science. It may not be history. But it is a compelling hu- man document. Important critics have long been at work. In Ashley Montagu's anthology they have their say once more, at length and in a permanent form. The net impression after going through these thirty reviews of the Study is, initially at all events, that not much has been left standing. Most of the articles (but not all) are excellent. These specialists have shown that the book will not stand in its various parts. The Western, the Chinese, the Islamic, the geographical evidence and conclusions have been torn to pieces. One admires the keen minds (if not always the mis- placed personal animus) behind this criticism. One may find one's self kneeling with Sir Ernest Barker to repeat "I believe in the national All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

REVIEWS OF BOOKS 257 State" (p. 96) or smiling with Mr. Lawrence Stone at the prospect of Toynbee "agile as a gibbon" skipping "rapidly from branch to branch of the historical tree, shaking down its mysterious fruit and arranging them in pre- determined patterns" (p. 113), but one may not be altogether surprised to find one's self keeping the volumes on one's shelf. The Study (it is Toynbee's own definition) is, after all, only "one person's impression of history in the new light in which we can now see it" (p. 4), and one accepts it as that. These acute demonstrations of the weaknesses of the work both in concep- tion and in execution do not destroy it. Difficult and maddening as it is to fight one's way through, the book is likely to continue to excite interest. And, wrongheaded though it may be, one is likely to go on peeping into its various parts for some time to come. At the very least, A study of history is a constant reminder of greater visions beyond our own tiny profes- sional world. JOHN C. CAIRNS University of Toronto THE DYNAMICS OF WORLD HISTORY. By Christo- pher Dawson. Edited by John J. Mulloy. New York: Sheed & Ward, 1957. Pp. 468. $6.00. This book comprises thirty-one essays (or excerpts from books) written by Christopher Dawson over a period of thirty-four years, to- gether with an interpretive essay on the con- tinuity and development of Dawson's thought from the pen of the editor. The collection is de- signed to support a thesis: to wit, that Christo- pher Dawson "has formulated a conception of world history that, in scope and vision, ranks with the work of Spengler, Northrop and Toyn- bee" (p. vii). Indeed, if I read the intent of the editor correctly, this volume is intended as a Roman Catholic answer to Toynbee's hetero- doxy and an antidote to his popularity in this country. Dawson most emphatically avoids any taint of heterodoxy. On the contrary, like many an- other convert, he tends sometimes to wear his faith on his sleeve. This aspect of his mind is clearest in the four essays grouped in this vol- ume under the heading "Christianity and the meaning of history," all of which are militantly Roman Catholic. Explicit affirmation of a theo- logical faith is relatively rare among historians today, and this introduces a distinctive, if com- pletely traditional, note into Dawson's work. More interesting, at least to this reviewer, is Dawson's effort to apply sociology to the il- lumination of history. Yet in these essays he does so only in a programmatic fashion. He offers a number of fascinating suggestions and illustrations but refrains from working out his ideas in any detail. This, I think, makes the claim of the preface absurd. Dawson's concep- tion of world history cannot rank with Speng- ler's or Toynbee's until he has made a sustained attempt to use the ideas and generalizations he throws off in these essays to construct a world history. This he is disinclined to attempt, on the ground that too many tracts of history remain unexplored or inadequately explored to permit anyone yet to write a real world history. His own more modest efforts have therefore cen- tered upon Europe. As he says: "Under the cir- cumstances the history of a single civilization seems the most that we can hope to achieve. It is here that European culture seems to offer the best starting point for an approach to world history, for its transforming influence on the other world cultures has been far greater than that of any of the Oriental civilizations" (p. 405). It is not possible to summarize Dawson's in- sights and suggestions about the interpretation of European or world history in a short review, all the more since the presentation of his ideas in this book is diffuse and disjointed, as one would expect from the diverse origins of the es- says. Suffice it to say that much of what he sug- gests seems sensible and occasionally brilliant. The editor's effort to systematize what Dawson says does not seem completely happy. The dis- jointedness remains, although occasionally eased by quotations from letters Dawson wrote to the editor, explaining or commenting upon his own work and identifying some of the men who influenced him in his youth. The really major question these essays raise, at least in my opinion, is one of intellectual jurisdiction. Dawson the sociologist and Daw- son the Catholic often seem to speak a rather different language. As a sociologist, for ex- ample, he can contemplate either the "complete secularization of Western culture" (p. 100) or "the coming of a new religion" or "the revival of the old religion with which the culture was formerly associated" (p. 101) as apparently equally possible courses for the future.
